case_study_insert.main_stem: Solstice Insulation Systems (SIS) is a private limited company in the sustainable building-materials sector, employing a workforce of 66. Founded in 2016 by Tomas Solstice, it makes recycled-cellulose insulation and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership on its production floor. SIS plans to invest $960,000 in a recycled-cellulose insulation line with low-energy manufacturing, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $560,000 from a new share issue. It has fixed costs of $504,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. SIS faces a production waste rate of 6.1% and rising quality complaints about inconsistent density, which Tomas wants cut before the new line starts.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The line produced 22,500 insulation batches last quarter with a waste rate of 6.1%, down from 8.0% a year earlier. Customer complaints about inconsistent density rose from 25 to 42 per month, and average delivery time is 4.4 days. Low-energy manufacturing trials cut power use per batch by 5.2%, while rejected batches numbered 31. A survey of 350 green builders found that 63% would pay up to $0.40 more for certified recycled insulation and 49% check environmental product declarations before specifying. A skills audit shows 19 of 66 staff lack training on the new line; accredited courses cost $690 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans such as SIS's $400,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.50 to $13.25 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in manufacturing. (3) Recycled-paper and fire-retardant additive input costs have risen 13.5% year-on-year, while green-building investment grew 7.2% and retrofit spending rose 3.9%.

questions.question_text: SIS plans to fund part of its $960,000 insulation line with a $400,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for SIS of using $560,000 from a new share issue instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $560,000 share issue provides equity with no interest or fixed repayment dates, so SIS avoids enlarging the $400,000 bank loan and protects cash flow while carrying $504,000 fixed costs and a 6.1% waste rate. Money not spent on loan interest can fund density checks on the new line, protecting the $16.00 selling price and 90,000-unit output and letting SIS act on the 63% of builders who will pay a premium.

Point 2: New equity strengthens the balance sheet and gives a wider capital base to absorb the risk of the $960,000 recycled-cellulose line, which is why a share issue was chosen over more debt. Unlike a larger loan, shares cannot be called in if the rising density complaints persist and cash generation slips. Although Tomas Solstice's ownership is diluted, the lower financial risk helps a young 66-employee manufacturer invest in training and quality while the line beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over a larger loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to SIS's expansion, existing loan and waste problem.

questions.question_text: SIS is launching certified recycled insulation. Consider green-building trade shows, social-media promotion, or direct specifications to architects. Which should SIS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Green-building trade shows: Exhibiting at sustainability events would bring SIS face to face with the 350 surveyed green builders and specifiers, allowing certificates and samples to be shown and supporting the $0.40 premium that 63% accept. Credibility is high. However, stand fees, travel and staff time are costly for a 66-employee firm funding a $960,000 line, and the audience is narrow and concentrated in a few cities.

Social-media promotion: Targeted online campaigns can reach the 49% who check environmental product declarations, are relatively cheap and give measurable engagement, and the message can spread quickly through the green-building sector that is growing by 7.2%. The drawback is that ad spend must be continuous, results depend on algorithms, and online enquiries convert less reliably than a specification written into a building project.

Direct specifications to architects: SIS representatives can present declarations and technical data to architects who specify materials, answering concerns about inconsistent density and securing the product into project schedules. This targets the 49% who check credentials and builds lasting relationships. It is slower to scale and uses staff time where 19 of 66 are still untrained.

Recommendation: SIS should choose direct specifications to architects, reinforced by limited social-media promotion. Direct specifications convert the 49% who check declarations and secure repeat project demand at low cost. Trade shows are rejected as expensive and geographically narrow; social media alone is rejected because it produces weaker commitments than a named specification.

SIS should further note that the 49% who check environmental declarations are specifiers whose trust is won by evidence, not by volume of advertising, so the chosen channel must carry the declaration data and the 5.2% energy saving; otherwise the $0.40 premium and the return on the $960,000 line will not materialise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to SIS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SIS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in context with a justified recommendation explaining why trade shows and social media alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: SIS's waste rate is 6.1% and quality complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for SIS of using its hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership to address these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A hierarchical structure gives SIS a clear chain of command from Tomas to the production floor, so one density standard can be imposed quickly to tackle the 6.1% waste rate and the complaints about inconsistent density. Autocratic leadership lets him halt off-spec batches immediately, protecting the $16.00 selling price and the 90,000-unit output needed to justify the $960,000 line.

Point 2: Clear roles and firm decisions let managers reallocate labour when 19 of 66 staff lack training, keeping the low-energy line running and limiting disruption to customers. Formal downward communication ensures every operator follows the same density checks, reducing the 42 monthly complaints. With fixed costs of $504,000 a year, this top-down control protects output and helps SIS act on the 49% of builders who check environmental declarations.

Tomas should also weigh that autocratic control can demotivate the 66 staff and worsen the quality complaints if operators feel unable to report density problems; the 19 untrained employees especially need clear instructions. The hierarchy therefore works only if the $690 training and firm standards are paired with reliable upward reporting.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of hierarchical/autocratic structures (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to SIS's waste, complaints, training gap and investment.

questions.question_text: SIS must train 19 staff on the new line. Consider accredited courses at $690 per employee or on-the-job coaching. Which should SIS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Accredited courses at $690 per employee: Formal training gives the 19 untrained staff a recognised standard in recycled-cellulose production and low-energy operation, which matters when density complaints have risen to 42 a month. The direct cost is $690 x 19 = $13,110, small beside the $960,000 investment. The drawbacks are lost production while staff attend and generic content that may not match SIS's exact machinery.

On-the-job coaching: Coaching on the line is equipment-specific, costs no fees and keeps all 19 staff productive, protecting output of 90,000 batches. Experienced operators can demonstrate the energy-saving routine from the 5.2% trial immediately. However, bad habits may spread, there is no external certificate to show green builders, and coaching can be disrupted by staff shortages.

Decision: SIS should choose accredited courses followed by on-site coaching. The qualification helps tackle the 6.1% waste rate and supports the certified positioning that 49% of builders check, and $13,110 is modest against $960,000. On-the-job coaching alone is rejected because it offers no recognised evidence of competence and is vulnerable to the density problem it is meant to fix.

Beyond the $690 fee, SIS must manage the 4.4-day delivery time while 19 staff train, so courses should be staggered. The real prize is quality: certification should reduce the 42 monthly density complaints and the 31 rejected batches, protecting the $16.00 price and the 63% willing to pay more. On-site coaching alone would leave no auditable evidence for the 49% checking declarations, which is why it loses. Tomas should also check that the staggered schedule still protects the 90,000-unit target.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SIS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of SIS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, certification and disruption, rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SIS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 72,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 90,000-unit output; premium pricing for the $0.40 eco premium; financing cover for the $960,000 line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $14.60 to cut waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $504,000 / ($16.00 - $9.00) = $504,000 / $7.00 = 72,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 72,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 - $9.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SIS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 72,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units gives a margin of safety of 18,000 units, showing the demand fall the $960,000 line can absorb.
2. Contribution of $7.00 lets managers value the $0.40 premium that 63% of builders accept: at $16.40 contribution becomes $7.40, justifying certification costs.
3. With $504,000 fixed costs and $7.00 contribution, managers can set the volume needed to service the $400,000 bank loan and $560,000 share issue.
4. Average total cost of $504,000 / 90,000 + $9.00 = $14.60 a unit provides a benchmark to detect whether the 6.1% waste rate is falling.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SIS's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has SIS's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 25.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 5.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 8.0%
ROCE 2024 = 10.0%
ROCE 2025 = 16.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $1,200,000 on revenue of $6,000,000 gives 20.0% in 2024; $1,875,000 on $7,500,000 gives 25.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $300,000 on $6,000,000 revenue is 5.0%, and $600,000 on $7,500,000 is 8.0% in 2025. Returns on the capital base are $300,000 / $3,000,000 = 10.0% and $600,000 / $3,750,000 = 16.0%.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The gross margin rose from 20.0% to 25.0%, so cost of sales took a smaller share of the $7,500,000 revenue, consistent with the 5.2% power saving in production. Operating margin improved from 5.0% to 8.0%, meaning operating profit more than doubled as revenue grew, despite the 6.1% waste rate and density complaints. The return on capital increased from 10.0% to 16.0%, so the extra $750,000 of capital employed is earning a better return. ROCE is the strongest evidence because it connects the $600,000 operating profit to the $3,750,000 capital employed, showing the $960,000 line is already being used productively; the gross margin could rise simply from cheaper recycled paper. Capital employed grew, so the higher return is not caused by a shrinking asset base. Interest payable rose only from $30,000 to $40,000, so financing costs are not driving the improvement.

Conclusion: SIS's financial performance has improved. All three measures moved favourably and the gains reflect stronger profit rather than accounting effects.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of margins and capital use and a justified conclusion, naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SIS of using low-energy manufacturing in its insulation line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Low-energy manufacturing cut power use per batch by 5.2% in the trial, reducing the $9.00 variable cost per unit and protecting the $7.00 contribution. It also strengthens the recycled, low-impact brand that 63% of surveyed builders will pay up to $0.40 more for and that 49% check through environmental declarations, supporting the $960,000 line and output of 90,000 batches.

Disadvantage: Low-energy equipment is capital-intensive and adds to the $504,000 fixed costs, and savings depend on reliable power and machinery uptime. The systems need specialist maintenance, and with 19 of 66 staff untrained and waste at 6.1%, a breakdown could disrupt the 31 rejected batches already recorded and delay delivery against a 4.4-day lead time, hurting the relationships with green builders.

Tomas should weigh the 5.2% power saving against the capital in the $960,000 budget and the $690 training cost, since the 42 density complaints show energy is not the only problem. If low-energy plant merely raises fixed costs while waste stays at 6.1%, the $7.00 contribution will not improve.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SIS's trial data, survey and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in recycled-paper and additive input costs will affect SIS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If SIS's $400,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $400,000 = $3,000, modest beside $504,000 fixed costs. If the loan is fixed-rate, the immediate cash effect is nil. Higher rates could still raise the cost of future borrowing and may slow the 7.2% growth in green-building investment.

Minimum wage rise (6.0%, to $13.25 per hour): SIS employs a workforce of 66 in production and packing roles largely paid hourly, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented; the defensible test is productivity of 90,000 units / 66 staff, about 1,364 batches per worker. If that holds, the rise is absorbable; if it falls, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (13.5% on recycled paper and additives): The insert does not decompose the $9.00 variable cost, so only a bounded figure is shown: if the whole variable cost rose 13.5%, that adds 13.5% x $9.00 = $1.215, about $1.22 a unit; across 90,000 units that is about $109,350 a year. Contribution would fall from $7.00 toward $5.78.

Conclusion: The 13.5% input-cost rise has the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that funds the $960,000 line and cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate. The interest rise is at most $3,000 and the wage rise can be offset by productivity; neither touches every unit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SIS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on SIS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a justified greatest-impact judgement rejecting the other two.
